# Basic Definitions {.center}

## Distribution {.center}

Describes the pattern of value/category outcomes for a variable or random process

## Describing a Distribution {.center}

-   [**Shape:**]{.underline} Symmetric, mound-shaped, skewed? How many "peaks"?

-   [**Center:**]{.underline} Where does the center of the pattern appear? Generally refers to mean, median, or mode

-   [**Variability:**]{.underline} How spread out is the distribution?

    -   Often described in terms of [**standard deviation**]{.underline}

-   [**Unusual data:**]{.underline} Are there any outliers?

## National Anthem Example {.center}

Dot plot of National Anthem length:

![](images/nadotplot.png){fig-alt="Dot plot of National Anthem length in seconds. Outliers include a dot at 64 seconds and dots at 154 and 156 seconds."}

## Data {.center}

Values measured or categories recorded on individual entities of interest.

## Observational Units {.center}

The individual entities on which the data is recorded.

## Variables {.center}

The recorded characteristics of the observational units.

## Quantitative (or Numerical) Data {.center}

Variables which take on numerical values

-   Ex: Height, age, number of pets, 40-yard dash time

## Qualitative (or Categorical) Data {.center}

Variables which take on category designations

-   Ex: Hair color, marital status, selecting A, B, or C on a multiple-choice question

## Symbol Comparison {.center}

<br> Symbols we use depend on our variable type:

|               |                          |                           |
|---------------|:------------------------:|:-------------------------:|
|               | **Categorical Variable** | **Quantitative Variable** |
| **Parameter** |          $\pi$           |           $\mu$           |
| **Statistic** |        $\hat{p}$         |         $\bar{x}$         |

. . .

<br>

Note: We only use sample standard deviation and standard deviation symbols ($s$, $\sigma$) when we are dealing with **quantitative variables.**

## Hypothesis Testing {.center}

-   Two hypotheses

-   Null hypothesis ($H_{0}$):

    -   The chance explanation, what we assume is true
    -   Uses =

-   Alternative hypothesis ($H_{A}$):

    -   What researchers think could be true
    -   Uses \>, \<, or ≠

We can either write our hypotheses in words or symbols.

# Strength of Evidence {.center}

## Strength of Evidence {.center}

Two methods for gathering strength of evidence so far:

-   P-value
-   Standardized statistic

We can obtain either of the above through simulation OR theory; we will mainly be using theory from here on out.

## Strength of Evidence {.center}

If we have strong evidence:

-   P-value is less than 0.05
-   Standardized statistic is outside the twos
-   We reject our null hypothesis, and accept the alternative

## Strength of Evidence {.center}

If we do NOT have strong evidence:

-   P-value is 0.05 or higher
-   Standardized statistic is inside the twos
-   We fail to null hypothesis, and cannot accept the alternative

## Standard Error (SE) {.center}

<br>

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
### SE for Proportions:

$$SE=\sqrt{\frac{\pi(1-\pi)}{n}}$$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### SE for Means:

$$SE=\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$
:::
:::::

## Standardized Statistic (SS) {.center}

<br>

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
### SS for Proportions:

$$z=\frac{\hat{p}-\pi}{SE}$$

$$=\frac{\hat{p}-\pi}{\sqrt{\frac{\pi(1-\pi)}{n}}}$$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### SS for Means:

$$t=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu}{SE}$$

$$=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu}{\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}}$$
:::
:::::

## Factors that impact evidence strength {.center}

1.  Distance between observed statistic & null value
2.  Sample size (n)
3.  One-sided or two-sided hypothesis test

## 1. Distance between observed statistic & null value {.center}

-   More distance between the observed statistic & null value = stronger evidence

-   Less distance between the observed statistic & null value = weaker evidence

## 2. Sample Size {.center}

-   Increasing sample size increases strength of evidence
-   Decreasing sample size decreases strength of evidence

## 3. One-sided or two-sided hypothesis test {.center}

-   One-sided test = stronger evidence
-   Two-sided test = weaker evidence

# Errors

## Type I Error {.center}

-   We reject the null hypothesis, but it is actually true
-   "False alarm"

## Type II Error {.center}

-   We fail to reject the null hypothesis, but it is actually false
-   "Missed opportunity"
